chunks: "I'd say it's true in a particular context, and the reason is transconductance.
A BJT's collector current is exponential in V BE , so its transconductance is g m equals I C over V T , about 39 mS at 1 milliamps, and it depends only on current and temperature.
A MOSFET in strong inversion has g m equals 2I D over V ov ; at the same 1 milliamps with a half-volt overdrive that's 4 mS, ten times less.
More g m per milliamp means more gain per stage, more gain-bandwidth per unit power, and lower voltage noise, because the input-referred thermal noise goes as one over g m .
The BJT's intrinsic gain, V A over V T , is also several thousand, versus a few hundred for a MOSFET.
And two BJTs' V BE match better than two MOSFETs' thresholds, which gives lower offset in differential pairs.

The downsides are that it draws base current, so the input resistance is finite, which matters with high-impedance sources, its exponential law is more nonlinear, and V BE and beta drift with temperature.
MOSFETs have an insulated gate, zero DC input current, better linearity per input volt, and they are what you get for free in a CMOS process.

So in discrete analog and precision or low-noise stages, BJTs are common; in integrated circuits MOSFETs dominate because of integration and power, and designers run them in weak inversion or use BiCMOS or JFET inputs when they need the best of both."
